# Helper library (generated)

Do-not-edit: generated from the docstrings in `src/helpers/` by `src/helpers/gen_docs.py`. Regenerating and getting a diff fails the build.

## masks_io

Verified mask I/O and timing facts (part 09).

The single decode/re-encode point for masks: SAM returns masks
compressed per frame, and this module is where they are stored and
reloaded. Agent code never parses ``.npz`` files itself.

It also owns the only sanctioned way for agent code to learn timing
(:func:`clip_facts`, enforces R-T1): frame count, measured fps, the
per-frame timestamp array, duplicate runs and cut indices — never a
container fps.

### `masks_io.save_masks`

```python
def save_masks(path, masks)
```

Save ``masks`` as one compressed ``.npz`` file.

``masks`` maps ``object_id`` (int or str) to ``{frame_index: bool
array}``. Every array must be 2-D; dtype is normalised to bool, so
a ``{object_id: {frame: bool array}}`` mapping round-trips
losslessly through :func:`load_masks` (same object ids with the
same int/str type, same int frame indices, identical pixels).

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"bad_masks"``, ``"bad_mask"``) on a
non-mapping input or a non-2-D array. Missing parent directories
are created.

### `masks_io.load_masks`

```python
def load_masks(path)
```

Load a ``.npz`` written by :func:`save_masks`.

Returns ``{object_id: {frame_index: bool array}}`` with int object
ids restored as int (evidence carries them as strings; the helpers
preserve int ids) and int frame indices. Arrays are bool dtype.

Raises ``OSError`` when the file is missing and ``ValueError``
(``"bad_masks_npz"``) when it is not a masks file.

### `masks_io.clip_facts`

```python
def clip_facts(timing_path)
```

The sanctioned timing facts for agent code (enforces R-T1).

Reads the part-05 timing report and returns ``{"frame_count",
"measured_fps", "timestamps", "duplicate_runs", "cut_indices"}``:
the frame count, the measured (never container) fps, the
per-frame timestamp array in seconds (a numpy array), duplicate
runs (each a sorted list of frame indices) and cut indices (a
sorted list).

Tolerates the report's key variants (``fps`` for ``measured_fps``,
``confirmed_duplicates`` for ``duplicate_runs``, ``cuts`` for
``cut_indices``). Raises ``OSError`` when the file is missing and
``ValueError`` (``"bad_timing"``) when it is malformed.

### `masks_io.read_frames`

```python
def read_frames(video_path, indices)
```

Decoded frames as arrays, in the order requested.

``indices`` are frame indices into the video; returns a list of
``uint8`` BGR arrays (OpenCV decode), one per requested index, in
the same order. Raises ``ValueError`` (``"no_such_video"``,
``"unreadable_frame"``) when the video cannot be opened or an
index cannot be decoded — never a neighbouring frame relabelled
as the requested one.

## tracks

Verified mask statistics and point tracks (part 09).

Pure functions over numpy arrays: per-frame statistics, the largest
connected piece, mask → tracked point, track quality flags, and
scene-relative tracks. Image coordinates: ``x`` grows right, ``y``
grows downward in pixels; the flip to metres-up happens in exactly
one place (:func:`src.helpers.physics.track_to_metres`), never here.

### `tracks.mask_stats`

```python
def mask_stats(mask)
```

Statistics for one frame's mask.

Returns ``{"top", "bottom", "left", "right", "height", "width",
"area", "centroid"}``: the extreme occupied rows/columns (ints,
inclusive), ``height = bottom - top + 1``, ``width = right - left
+ 1``, the occupied pixel count, and ``centroid`` as ``{"x",
"y"}`` floats (mean occupied column/row). Raises ``ValueError``
(``"empty_mask"``) on an empty mask — never zeros that look like a
measurement at the origin.

### `tracks.largest_component`

```python
def largest_component(mask)
```

Keep the largest connected piece of a mask.

OpenCV connected components; returns a bool array with only the
largest component set. A stray blob must not move "the bottom of
the body". Raises ``ValueError`` (``"empty_mask"``) on an empty
mask.

### `tracks.track_point`

```python
def track_point(masks, mode, timestamps = None)
```

Per-frame track of a chosen point.

``masks`` maps ``frame_index`` to a mask; ``mode`` is one of
``centroid``, ``bottom_centre`` (mean-x at the bottom row),
``top_centre`` (mean-x at the top row) or ``lowest_point`` (the
bottom-most occupied pixel; ties averaged). ``timestamps`` maps
``frame_index`` to video seconds; when omitted, ``t`` is the
frame index as a float.

Returns ``{"frame", "t", "x_px", "y_px", "mode"}`` rows sorted by
frame. Empty frames are skipped (the gap shows up in
:func:`track_quality`); when no frame yields a point, raises
``ValueError`` (``"empty_mask"``). An unknown mode raises
``ValueError`` (``"bad_mode"``).

### `tracks.track_quality`

```python
def track_quality(track, masks_by_object, jump_heights_per_frame = 1.0)
```

Quality flags for a track against its masks.

``track`` is :func:`track_point` rows; ``masks_by_object`` maps
``object_id`` to ``{frame_index: mask}``. The tracked object is
the rows' ``"object_id"`` when present, else the sole object;
when several objects are present and the rows name none, split
flags are evaluated over every object.

Returns ``{"gaps", "jumps", "splits", "identity_swaps", "ok"}``:

- **gaps:** frames missing between the first and last tracked
  frame;
- **jumps:** frames whose displacement from the previous tracked
  frame exceeds ``jump_heights_per_frame`` mask-heights per frame
  (normalised by the frame gap, so a gap is not itself a jump);
- **splits:** frames where the second-largest component exceeds
  25% of the largest (posture split or a second object bleeding
  in);
- **identity_swaps:** frames where some object's self-IoU with
  its previous mask drops below the identity-swap threshold while
  its IoU with another object's previous mask exceeds the
  self-IoU — SAM object ids are unstable when objects overlap, so
  a flagged segment must be re-tracked or excluded, not trusted.

``"ok"`` is true when every flag list is empty.

### `tracks.relative_track`

```python
def relative_track(track_a, track_b)
```

A's positions minus B's, aligned on common frames.

For a wall run this is the runner relative to a track fixed on
the wall, which enforces R-M3 mechanically. Returns ``{"frame",
"t", "x_px", "y_px"}`` rows (``t`` from A) sorted by frame.
Raises ``ValueError`` (``"no_common_frames"``) when the tracks
share no frame.

### `tracks.find_still_patches`

```python
def find_still_patches(video_path, frames, avoid = None, size = 64, count = 3)
```

Boxes of background that no moving thing crosses.

Returns up to ``count`` boxes ``(x, y, w, h)`` of ``size``×``size``
pixels. A box qualifies only if, grown by 20 px on every side, it
does not meet the bounding box of any mask in ``avoid`` (masks by
object, as :func:`src.helpers.masks_io.load_masks` returns them)
on any of ``frames``. Frames that a mask does not cover are not
checked for that mask. Among the qualifying boxes on the first of
``frames``, the ones with the most texture (variance of the
Laplacian of the grey image) are returned, with centres at least
``2·size`` apart (greedy, most textured first). When nothing
qualifies, returns ``[]``.

How to use this for ``camera.still``: pass every frame of the fit
window and the masks of every moving thing as ``avoid``; take the
first box returned here, track it with :func:`still_track`, save
the rows as a workspace JSON file and cite that file as
``reference_track_artifact``. A template tracked by hand next to
a moving thing follows it and reads as camera motion — these
patches are clear of every mover by construction instead.

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"no_such_video"``,
``"unreadable_frame"``, ``"bad_frames"``, ``"bad_box"``) on
unusable inputs.

### `tracks.still_track`

```python
def still_track(video_path, frames, box, avoid = None)
```

Track a fixed background patch across frames.

``box`` is ``(x, y, w, h)`` — usually the first box from
:func:`find_still_patches`. Returns one row per frame in
``frames``, in order, with exactly the keys ``frame``, ``x_px``
and ``y_px`` (the same row format as a
``reference_track_artifact``): the box centre on the first of
``frames`` plus, per frame, the shift of the box's grey patch from
the first of ``frames`` measured by phase correlation with a Hann
window (sub-pixel).

The box is first checked with the same ``avoid`` test as
:func:`find_still_patches` (grown by 20 px on every side against
every mover's bounding box on each of ``frames``); when the box
meets a mover, raises ``ValueError`` (``"mover_overlap"``) naming
the object and the frame, for example ``"mover_overlap: box meets
object 'pole' on frame 12"``.

How to use this for ``camera.still``: pass every frame of the fit
window and the masks of every moving thing as ``avoid``; save the
returned rows as a workspace JSON file and cite that file as
``reference_track_artifact``. A template tracked by hand next to
a moving thing follows it and reads as camera motion — this
measures the patch the library verified is clear of movers.

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"no_such_video"``,
``"unreadable_frame"``, ``"bad_frames"``, ``"bad_box"``,
``"mover_overlap"``) on unusable inputs.

## physics

Verified gravity, scale and ghost arithmetic (part 09).

Pure functions over numpy arrays. Image coordinates grow downward in
pixels; physics works in metres with ``y`` up. The conversion happens
in exactly one place (:func:`track_to_metres`), so sign errors have
one home. Time is always seconds from measured timestamps — no helper
accepts a container fps.

### `physics.fit_parabola`

```python
def fit_parabola(t, y_m)
```

Least-squares ``y = y0 + v0·t + ½·a·t²``.

Returns ``{"y0", "v0", "a", "g_app", "g_app_sigma", "rmse",
"residuals", "residual_trend", "residual_trend_z", "n"}``: the
fitted intercept, initial velocity and acceleration ``a`` (hence
``g_app = |a|``), its sigma from the residual sum of squares with
honest degrees of freedom (``n - 3``), the root-mean-square
residual, the residual series, the sample count, and two residual
trend statistics (see below).

A large residual trend is the signature of a non-rigid tracked
point (R-M2) and is returned, never hidden. It is *not* the slope
of residuals vs. time: least-squares residuals are orthogonal to
every design column, and ``t`` is one of them, so that slope is
zero by construction and can never fire. Instead:

- ``residual_trend`` is the correlation between the residuals and
  the centred cubic term ``(t - t̄)³`` made orthogonal to the
  design columns ``(1, t, t²)`` — the partial correlation of a
  cubic term. Near zero for one stretch of constant acceleration;
  large in magnitude when the window mixes phases (support, a
  change of surface, a turn) or the tracked point deforms.
- ``residual_trend_z`` is the ``|t|`` statistic of the cubic
  coefficient ``j`` in the extended fit ``y = y0 + v0·t + ½·a·t²
  + j·t³``, computed on the same points as the fit. A
  ``residual_trend_z`` above 3 means the window is not one stretch
  of constant acceleration: it mixes phases or the tracked point
  deforms. (With only 4 points the cubic addition consumes all
  freedom, so ``residual_trend_z`` is reported as 0.0.)

When the fit is exact to floating-point dust (rmse below 1e-9 of
the data span) both statistics are 0.0: the correlation of rounding
error is arbitrary, not a measurement.

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"short_track"``) on fewer than 4 points
and (``"degenerate_track"``) when the time base is degenerate.

### `physics.scale_from_reference`

```python
def scale_from_reference(extent_px, extent_px_sigma, size_m, size_m_sigma)
```

Metres per pixel from a reference of known size.

``m_per_px = size_m / extent_px`` with standard propagation
``σ = m·√((σ_px/extent_px)² + (σ_m/size_m)²)``. Returns
``(m_per_px, sigma)`` as floats — always a pair where an error is
meaningful. Raises ``ValueError`` (``"bad_scale"``) on
non-positive or non-finite inputs.

### `physics.track_to_metres`

```python
def track_to_metres(track, m_per_px, origin)
```

Pixel track → metres, flipping ``y``.

The one home of the sign flip: image ``y`` grows downward, physics
works in metres with ``y`` up, so ``y_m = (origin_y - y_px) ·
m_per_px`` and ``x_m = (x_px - origin_x) · m_per_px``. ``origin``
is ``{"x_px", "y_px"}`` (a tuple/list ``(x, y)`` also works),
usually the takeoff pixel. ``m_per_px`` is a bare number or a
``(value, sigma)`` pair.

Returns ``{"rows", "m_per_px", "sigma_m_per_px", "origin_px"}``:
rows are ``{"frame", "t", "x_m", "y_m"}``. Errors are carried as
the single scale-relative term ``sigma_m_per_px``; per-point
pixel noise is the fit's job, not this function's.

### `physics.worlds_fit`

```python
def worlds_fit(g_app, sigma, candidate_worlds)
```

Native-speed fit arithmetic over the candidate worlds.

For each candidate ``{"name", "g"}`` (``"g_m_s2"`` is accepted as
an alias): ``delta_sigma = |g - g_app| / sigma`` and
``fits_native = delta_sigma <= 2`` (part 02 §4); ``retime_factor =
√(g_world / g_app)`` — the slow-down that would map the measured
gravity onto that world — is reported per candidate as pure
arithmetic (``None`` when ``g_app`` is not positive, never a
guessed number). This function contains no scene judgement: which
candidates are even considered (R-W1) lives in validation.

Returns a list of ``{"name", "g", "delta_sigma", "fits_native",
"retime_factor"}``. Raises ``ValueError`` (``"bad_gravity"``,
``"bad_sigma"``, ``"bad_world"``) on unusable inputs.

### `physics.ghost`

```python
def ghost(takeoff_state, g_ghost, m_per_px, t_grid, land_y_m = 0.0)
```

Propagate a takeoff state under ``g_ghost``.

``takeoff_state`` is ``{"x0", "y0", "vx", "vy"}`` in metres with
``y`` up; ``g_ghost`` the (positive) gravity to integrate under;
``t_grid`` the grid of times (seconds, takeoff-relative) at which
to sample the path; ``land_y_m`` the landing height in metres
relative to the takeoff point with ``y`` up (a landing below
takeoff gives a negative ``land_y_m``). Returns ``{"path",
"landing"}``: path entries are ``{"t", "x_m", "y_m", "x_px",
"y_px"}`` (pixel equivalents are relative to the metre origin via
``m_per_px``), and landing is where the path, after its peak,
reaches the height ``land_y_m``, at ``t_land = (vy + sqrt(vy² -
2·g·land_y_m)) / g``. With ``land_y_m = 0`` this is today's
``2·vy/g``, so every existing call keeps its result. The path is
sampled on the grid up to ``t_land``, and the exact landing point
is always appended, even between grid samples. When the path peaks
below ``land_y_m`` (``vy² < 2·g·land_y_m``), the landing falls back
to the return to takeoff height. (Part 11 decides *which* gravity
the ghost uses; this just integrates.)

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"no_takeoff"``) when ``vy <= 0`` — the
path never returns to takeoff height — and (``"bad_gravity"``,
``"bad_scale"``, ``"short_grid"``, ``"bad_landing"``) on unusable
inputs.

## clock

Verified gait clock (part 09).

The gait signal and the step-rate clock. This is the signal that
worked — head-bob is not implemented anywhere in the library (R-C2).

### `clock.gait_signal`

```python
def gait_signal(masks)
```

Per-frame gait signal from a mask series.

``masks`` maps ``frame_index`` to a mask. For each frame the
signal is the width of the **lowest 30% of the mask rows** (from
the bottom of the mask's span upward) divided by the mask height:
``(max occupied column - min occupied column + 1) / height`` over
that row band. Legs spreading and closing modulate this width
once per stride cycle.

Returns ``{"frame", "gait"}`` rows sorted by frame. Raises
``ValueError`` (``"empty_mask"``) when a frame's mask is empty —
a missing body is not a zero-width measurement.

### `clock.step_rate`

```python
def step_rate(signal, t, band_hz = None)
```

Step-rate clock from a gait signal.

Detrends ``signal`` with a **running median** (window from config,
odd, ~1 s — this removes the slow perspective trend without
touching the stepping oscillation), then takes a simple
periodogram/FFT peak search **strictly inside** ``band_hz``
(default 1–4 Hz). ``t`` holds the sample times in seconds.

Returns ``(result, flag)``:

- on success, ``result`` is ``{"peak_hz", "as_step_hz",
  "as_stride_hz", "alt_step_hz", "harmonic_evidence", "band_hz"}``
  and ``flag`` is None. The peak is read two ways, because R-C3's
  ambiguity is data, not a silent choice: reading A takes the
  peak as the step rate (``as_step_hz = peak``,
  ``as_stride_hz = peak / 2``); reading B takes the peak as the
  stride rate (``alt_step_hz = 2 × peak``). ``harmonic_evidence``
  reports the spectrum power at the peak, at double and at half
  the peak (nearest bins, evidence only — never returned as a
  rate) with their ratios, so the choice between readings stays
  checkable.
- when the peak sits at a band edge (the lowest or highest
  in-band bin, or within 1.5 bins of the band boundary — the
  peak is then unresolved from the boundary), the peak is not
  clamped into a number: returns ``(None, "no_reliable_clock")``.
  A frequency outside the band is never returned, and an edge
  peak is never promoted.

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"short_signal"``) on fewer than 8
samples, (``"bad_timebase"``) on unusable times, (``"bad_band"``)
on an unusable band, and (``"peak_at_band_edge"``) when the
sampling cannot place a single bin strictly inside the band (the
peak would be pinned at the edge by construction).

### `clock.clock_evidence`

```python
def clock_evidence(rate, signal_description, interpretation, natural_range_hz, natural_range_source, band_hz, window_frames, method)
```

The evidence ``clock`` object, built by the library (part 09 §7).

``rate`` is :func:`step_rate`'s result — either its result dict
or its ``(result, flag)`` pair. A ``None`` result, or a pair
whose flag is not None (the band-edge ``"no_reliable_clock"``),
raises ``ValueError`` (``"no_reliable_clock"``): an edge peak is
never promoted into a clock. ``interpretation`` picks the
reading: ``"step"`` reports ``as_step_hz``, ``"stride"`` reports
``as_stride_hz`` — R-C3's ambiguity stays an explicit choice.

``natural_range_hz`` is stored as ``[lo, hi]``; a ``{min, max}``
mapping (the shape wall runs 9 and 10 wrote) is accepted and
converted. ``natural_range_source`` is ``{"url", "quote"}``.
``band_hz`` is the search band, stored as ``[lo, hi]``.
``window_frames`` is the analysed window's frame count (a
positive int) and ``method`` names the estimation procedure (a
nonempty string); both are validated here and feed the quoted
σ, not stored — the contract's ``clock`` shape carries no other
fields.

The quoted ``measured_rate_sigma_hz`` is half the search-band
width spread over ``√window_frames`` independent bins: a
resolution term from the window the peak was picked in, so longer
windows quote tighter clocks.

``signal_description`` says what was timed (for example the
lowest-thirty-percent width signal). Every parameter is
required: a missing one raises ``ValueError`` naming that field
(``"rate"``, ``"signal_description"``, ``"interpretation"``,
``"natural_range_hz"``, ``"natural_range_source"``,
``"band_hz"``, ``"window_frames"``, ``"method"``).

Returns exactly the evidence ``clock`` shape (part 12):
``signal_description``, ``measured_rate_hz``,
``measured_rate_sigma_hz``, ``interpretation``, ``band_hz``,
``natural_range_hz``, ``natural_range_source`` — nothing more,
so it validates against the contract's ``clock`` schema.

## ranges

Range-check building blocks (part 09 §7).

Part 11 checks every range check the hard way (``RANGE_EXTENT_NOT_ON_MASK``,
``RANGE_FORMULA_MISMATCH``, ``RANGE_SIGMA_TOO_SMALL``,
``RANGE_NUMBER_WITHOUT_PROVENANCE``); this module makes the right numbers
the easy ones. Pure functions over numpy arrays and plain values — no model
calls, no network — with no I/O except printing (so the ``run_python`` call
that prints a check is the check's ``measurement_artifact``).

Time is never involved here; image coordinates grow downward in pixels,
and a length is a pixel distance until :func:`range_value` applies the
scale.

### `ranges.mask_extent`

```python
def mask_extent(mask, direction = None)
```

The two mask pixels farthest apart along ``direction``.

Returns ``{"x1", "y1", "x2", "y2", "length_px"}``: integer pixel
coordinates of both endpoints and their Euclidean distance. Both
endpoints are mask pixels by construction — the pair of True
pixels maximising the projected distance along ``direction`` — so
a check built from them passes part 11's
``RANGE_EXTENT_NOT_ON_MASK`` on geometry alone.

``direction`` is a unit vector ``(dx, dy)`` in image coordinates
(``y`` grows downward), such as ``(0, 1)`` for a vertical extent.
With ``None`` the mask's principal axis (first principal
component of the pixel cloud) is used.

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"empty_mask"``) on an empty mask and
``ValueError`` (``"bad_direction"`` / ``"bad_mask"``) on an
unusable direction or input.

### `ranges.range_value`

```python
def range_value(kind, extents, m_per_px = None, m_per_px_sigma = None)
```

A range-check value recomputed exactly as part 11 §20 does.

Returns ``{"value", "sigma", "formula", "uses_scale"}``:

- ``kind="ratio"`` takes two extents: ``value`` is
  ``extents[0].length_px / extents[1].length_px`` and ``formula``
  is ``"<name0>_px / <name1>_px"`` (for example ``"palm_px /
  hand_px"``);
- ``kind="length"`` takes one extent and the scale: ``value`` is
  ``length_px × m_per_px`` and ``formula`` is ``"length_px ×
  m_per_px"``.

``sigma`` propagates 1 px per endpoint (``√2`` px per extent, in
quadrature over the extents), plus the scale's relative ``σ`` for
a length — the same floor part 11's ``RANGE_SIGMA_TOO_SMALL``
demands, so a value built here clears it by construction.

Raises ``ValueError`` (``"bad_kind"``) on another kind,
``ValueError`` (``"bad_extent"``) on a missing or unusable
extent, and ``ValueError`` (``"bad_scale"``) on a missing or
unusable scale for a length.

### `ranges.print_check`

```python
def print_check(item)
```

Print a range check as one JSON line, and return that line.

Every number the evidence cites — the value, its σ and every
extent endpoint — is in the printed line, so the ``run_python``
call that prints it is the check's ``measurement_artifact`` and
part 11's ``RANGE_NUMBER_WITHOUT_PROVENANCE`` is satisfied by
construction. Keys are sorted for stable output.
